Rosa entered the courtroom staring straight ahead, her kerchief perfectly tied and a polite smile on her face. But as she got closer to the designated bench, you could see a slight tremor in her step.

She sat down and opened her mouth to speak. There were a few seconds of silence; Rosa’s mouth remained slightly open and her lower lip quivered. Finally, a slight gasp came out, and a single tear rolled down her cheek.

Rosa took a deep breath. “I … I have something to tell the Rav. In private.”

Rav Yechezkel motioned to the shamash. “Get her some water,” he murmured, shooing him away with the back of his hand. Once the shamash was out of earshot, he turned back to Rosa. “Yes.”

“Was it frightening?” Rav Yechezkel gently prodded.

Just then, the shamash returned with a jug of water. “Drink, drink,” said Rav Yechezkel. He paused, waited for her to finish the glass, and sent the shamash on another errand. “I have a feeling … Well, for your sake, it is best if

you relay your dream. As for my message, it can wait.”

LAST TIME: Yosef, a young businessman from Cracow, is murdered on the way back from a business trip, leaving his wife, Rosa, a widow. After a year of no marriage prospects for Rosa, Reb Yosef Yuzpa, an old parush, tells the rav that he wishes to marry her. The Surprise

My father appeared to me, just as I remembered him before he passed away … dressed in his Shabbos best. He told me, ’Mazal tov! I have heard in Shamayim that you are to be married!’

As I said, I’m still not sure I believe it myself. Oh, this must be pure nonsense. But the dream, it felt so real … Honorable Rav, my father told me that I must marry the old parush, Reb Yosef Yuzpa.”

between Purim and Pesach, as the wildflowers began to bloom, Rosa stood before the entire community for a second time. But now, instead of standing for her chalitza, she was standing under a chuppah. She was marrying a second Yosef.

Rosa’s wedding to the first Yosef had been a lavish affair.

Her father was able to afford tables so long and wide that it practically took a minyan of men to lift them. Silken tablecloths and mounds of food bedecked the festive tables—so much, that the leftovers had fed Cracow’s poor for the entire week to follow.

In contrast, this second celebration was very simple. The chuppah took place on the

grass in front of the shul. A few of the guests sat on wooden benches borrowed from inside,

while most watched from the side alley. The seudah consisted of whatever food the guests brought from home.

Despite the modest arrangements, as Rosa stood beside her chosson, she felt like the richest woman in the world. What could be more valuable than the promise that her shidduch was made in Shamayim? She had her father’s word that marrying Reb Yosef Yuzpa would bring her tremendous bracha.

Exactly one year after their marriage, the bracha came to be: Rosa gave birth to a healthy baby boy. The community tzedakah fund supported the young couple, allowing both Rosa and her new husband to devote their days to what they loved: Reb Yosef Yuzpa, to learning on his beloved bench in the beis midrash, and Rosa, to rocking, feeding, and caring for her precious son, whom they had named Eliyahu — after the navi.

Before Eliyahu turned three, Reb Yosef Yuzpa declared that it was time for the boy to begin learning Torah.
